transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A school district in California has announced plans to integrate artificial intelligence tutoring systems into its middle school mathematics curriculum starting this fall. The district will spend approximately 2.3 million dollars on the AI program, which provides personalized learning paths for students based on their individual performance. District officials say the AI tutor can identify gaps in understanding and offer customized practice problems, allowing teachers to focus more on one-on-one support for students who need extra help. A pilot program conducted last year at three schools showed that students using the AI system improved their test scores by an average of 18 percent compared to the previous year. However, some teachers have expressed concerns about over-reliance on technology and the potential reduction in human interaction. The district says teachers will receive specialized training before the program launches and will maintain full control over their lesson plans.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: City officials in London have announced that five major public libraries will begin operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week starting in September. The extended hours initiative is aimed at serving shift workers, students with irregular study schedules, and homeless individuals seeking a safe place during nighttime hours. The program will cost an estimated 4 million pounds annually, with funding coming from the city's budget and private donations. In addition to extended hours, the libraries will add new services including overnight computer access, free coffee after midnight, and dedicated quiet zones for sleeping. Library staff will be supplemented by security personnel and social workers during overnight shifts to ensure safety and connect people in need with community resources. Mayor Catherine Robinson stated that libraries are essential public spaces that should be accessible to everyone regardless of their schedule. Other cities across the UK are reportedly considering similar measures based on London's example.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Authorities in Singapore have unveiled an ambitious urban greening plan that aims to plant one million trees across the city-state over the next decade. The initiative, called "City in Nature," seeks to reduce urban heat island effects, improve air quality, and provide residents with more recreational green spaces. The government has allocated 1.5 billion Singapore dollars for the project, which will include creating new parks, planting trees along roadsides, and installing vertical gardens on public housing buildings. Singapore already has a reputation as one of Asia's greenest cities, with nearly 50 percent of its land area covered in greenery. However, officials say climate change and population growth make additional greening efforts necessary. The plan also includes provisions for community involvement, encouraging residents to participate in tree-planting events and adopt neighborhood green spaces. Experts predict the project could reduce average urban temperatures by up to two degrees Celsius once completed.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Richard): Excuse me, Professor Carter? Do you have a few minutes? I wanted to ask you about the undergraduate research scholarship application.
Woman (Professor Carter): Of course, Richard. Come in, have a seat. Are you thinking about applying this semester?

Man: Yes, I am. I'm really interested in the research project you mentioned last week about renewable energy policies, and I was hoping to apply to work on that. But I'm a bit confused about the application requirements. The website says we need two letters of recommendation—do both of those have to be from professors?

Woman: One should be from a faculty member who can speak to your academic abilities, preferably someone in your major. The other can be from an employer or a supervisor from a volunteer position, as long as they can talk about your work ethic and reliability. Since you've done well in my environmental policy class, I'd be happy to write one for you.
Man: That's great to hear, thank you so much! I was also wondering about the personal statement. The guidelines say it should be 500 words—what exactly should I focus on?

Woman: You should explain why you're interested in this particular research area, any relevant experience you have—even if it's just coursework—and what you hope to gain from the experience. Don't just list your achievements; tell a story that shows your passion for the subject. Also, be specific about why you want to work on this project rather than any other.
Man: Okay, that makes sense. What about the deadline? The website said March 15th, but I heard someone mention it had been extended.

Woman: Yes, actually, the deadline was pushed back to March 22nd because of the winter storm that closed campus last week. That gives you an extra week. But don't wait until the last minute—you want to give your recommenders plenty of time to write their letters. I'd ask them at least two weeks before the deadline.
Man: I'll make sure to do that. One more thing—if selected, how many hours per week would I be expected to work on the project?

Woman: It's about 10 hours a week during the semester, which works out nicely with your class schedule. It's paid, too—15 dollars an hour, and you can arrange your hours around your classes. And if you do good work, there's often an opportunity to continue over the summer with a full-time stipend.
Man: That sounds perfect. Thank you so much for your help, Professor Carter. I really appreciate it.
Woman: You're very welcome, Richard. I think you'd be an excellent addition to the project. Get your application in, and I look forward to reading it.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Christopher): Hey Laura, have you made any plans for spring break yet? A bunch of us are thinking about going camping in the national park.
Woman (Laura): Oh, that sounds like fun! I was actually considering visiting my sister in Chicago, but camping could be really nice too. How many people are going?

Man: So far, there's me, Mark, Sarah, and Jennifer—we're trying to get a group of six or seven. We thought about renting a couple of those log cabins in the park instead of pitching tents, since the weather can still be pretty unpredictable in March.
Woman: Cabins would definitely be more comfortable. Do they have heating? I'm not really into the idea of freezing at night.

Man: Yeah, the ones we looked at have electric heaters and even a small kitchen area with a fridge and microwave. They're pretty basic, but way nicer than sleeping on the ground in a tent. The cost would be about 80 dollars per person for three nights if we can get eight people to come.
Woman: That's reasonable. When exactly were you thinking of going? I have a midterm on the Thursday before break, so I wouldn't be able to leave until that Friday afternoon.

Man: We were planning to leave Friday morning, but we could easily push it back to Friday afternoon to accommodate you. We'd come back Monday evening, so that's three full nights. Sarah's family has a couple of large coolers we can borrow for food and drinks.
Woman: What about food? Are we planning to cook at the campsite?

Man: That's the idea—we thought we'd do a grocery run together before we leave and split the cost. There are grills at the campsite, so we could do burgers and hot dogs one night, maybe pasta another night. And of course, s'mores by the campfire!
Woman: I love s'mores! Wait, do we need any special permits or reservations? I've heard the park gets really busy during spring break.

Man: Mark already looked into that—he reserved two adjacent campsites with cabin access back in January. They were going fast, so he jumped on it early. We just need to pay him our share of the reservation fee by the end of this week. That's 20 dollars per person to lock in our spot.

Woman: That's smart planning. I think I'm in! Let me just check my work schedule—I have a part-time job at the bookstore, but I'm pretty sure I can get those days off. I'll confirm with you tomorrow, is that okay?
Man: Perfect! Just let me know as soon as you can so we can finalize numbers and start planning meals.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: In today's fast-paced world, getting enough sleep has become a luxury for many people rather than a necessity. However, research consistently shows that sleep deprivation has serious consequences for both physical and mental health. Adults typically need between seven and nine hours of sleep per night, yet studies indicate that more than 30 percent of adults regularly get fewer than six hours. The effects of insufficient sleep extend far beyond feeling tired the next day. One of the most immediate impacts is on cognitive function—sleep-deprived individuals show reduced attention span, poorer decision-making abilities, and decreased creativity. This can be particularly dangerous when driving; drowsy driving causes thousands of accidents each year, with reaction times similar to those of someone under the influence of alcohol. Long-term sleep deprivation has been linked to more serious health problems including weakened immune system function, increased risk of heart disease and diabetes, and weight gain. When we sleep, our bodies produce hormones that regulate appetite and metabolism; without adequate rest, these hormones become imbalanced, leading to increased cravings for sugary and high-fat foods. Sleep also plays a crucial role in emotional regulation. People who don't get enough sleep are more likely to experience mood swings, anxiety, and symptoms of depression. Experts recommend establishing a consistent sleep schedule, avoiding screens for at least an hour before bed, and creating a dark, quiet sleep environment to improve sleep quality.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: More than half of the world's population is bilingual or multilingual, speaking two or more languages with varying degrees of fluency. While many people learn second languages for practical reasons such as work or travel, research shows that being bilingual offers significant cognitive benefits that extend throughout life. One of the most well-documented advantages is improved executive function—the set of mental skills that includes attention control, task switching, and working memory. Bilingual individuals constantly switch between languages and suppress one language while using another, which exercises these mental muscles. This enhanced cognitive control shows up even in tasks that have nothing to do with language. Studies have found that bilingual children are better at focusing on instructions and ignoring distractions in the classroom, abilities that contribute to academic success. Bilingual adults also tend to show delayed onset of dementia and Alzheimer's disease by an average of four to five years compared to monolinguals, even when brain scans show similar levels of disease progression. Researchers believe this is because bilingualism builds up what's called "cognitive reserve," allowing the brain to compensate for damage more effectively. Contrary to outdated beliefs that learning two languages confuses children, recent research indicates that bilingual children actually develop stronger metalinguistic awareness—the ability to think about language as a system. This can make learning additional languages easier in the future and improve overall communication skills. In our increasingly globalized world, bilingualism offers not only practical advantages but also meaningful cognitive benefits that make it a valuable skill at any age.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: The pandemic accelerated a trend that was already underway: small businesses across the world are undergoing digital transformation at an unprecedented pace. What used to be considered optional—having an online presence, accepting digital payments, offering delivery or curbside pickup—has become essential for survival. According to a recent survey by the Small Business Administration, 78 percent of small businesses in the United States have increased their use of digital tools since 2020, and 62 percent say these changes are permanent. For many traditional businesses like restaurants, retail shops, and local service providers, this shift has meant building websites, creating social media profiles, and adopting e-commerce platforms for the first time. Digital tools offer small businesses several advantages beyond simply surviving. They allow businesses to reach customers beyond their local area—for example, a craft bakery in a small town can now ship products nationwide. Customer relationship management software helps business owners track preferences and provide personalized service that large chain stores often can't match. Digital payment systems reduce the risks of handling cash and make transactions faster and more convenient. However, digital transformation also presents challenges. Many small business owners lack technical expertise and struggle with choosing the right tools, managing online reviews, and protecting against cybersecurity threats. The cost of digital tools can also be burdensome for businesses operating on thin margins. Despite these challenges, experts agree that digital adoption is no longer optional for small businesses. Governments and business organizations are increasingly offering free training programs and grants to help small businesses make this transition successfully.
